newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Izetbegovic says minister to go under US 'diktat'.
newsitem.headline: Izetbegovic says minister to go under US 'diktat'.

text.p: President Alija Izetbegovic of Bosnia said on Sunday a senior defence official would be removed to comply with a U.S. "diktat" imposed as a condition for $100 million in military aid to the Bosnian Federation.

Izetbegovic, in an interview with official BH Press, expressed displeasure at the U.S. demand for the dismissal of Bosnian deputy defence minister Hasan Cengic, but said he would go in the interests of good relations with Washington.

The military hardware, which includes tanks, artillery batteries and helicopters for Bosnia's postwar Moslem-Croat Federation, arrived almost two weeks ago by ship at the port of Ploce in neighbouring Croatia.

But the vessel moved offshore without unloading after Bosnian authorities baulked at firing Cengic, a Moslem nationalist with close ties to Iran, which is said by Washington to be an orchestrator of Islamic terrorism.

Asked by BH Press how the Cengic problem would be resolved, Izetbegovic said, "By the only possible way -- changes in government in the scope of normal reconstruction of government following elections. He will get some other field of activity."

Bosnian government sources said earlier the Federation parliament would probably bump Cengic from the defence ministry this week when it names a new government but retain him for another senior post unconnected to the military.

Bosnian officials have bridled at pressure to sack Cengic since he was instrumental in securing weapons from Islamic countries and others to help defend Sarajevo from besieging Serbs in the 1992-95 war, circumventing a U.N. arms embargo.

Izetbegovic, a Moslem, made no secret of his unhappiness with the U.S. demand, which he described as "a diktat". He complained that Washington had led Sarajevo to believe all conditions for the arms shipment were met some time ago.
"All conditions were fulfilled (earlier). Changes in the defence ministry were an additional U.S. request," he said.
But Izetbegovic added that his government realised U.S. patronage was more important for Bosnia than that of Iran.
"They requested us to stop military cooperation with Iran and we have done that. We do not conduct two-faced politics.

"We had to choose between military cooperation with America or with Iran, because we could not choose both. We chose military cooperation with America because we estimated they could give us more guarantees against a repetition of (Serb) aggression in the future," Izetbegovic said.

"We have no reasons to be ashamed...Some people from our surroundings expect us to stick out our tongue at America so that it (America) could ride us afterwards. We will not give (anyone) that pleasure," the Moslem leader said.
"After all is measured, America is our better friend."

The U.S.-conceived "Equip and Train" programme, entailing weapons shipments and instruction in modern warfare, is meant to help the Federation attain military parity with the Serb republic entity in Bosnia.

Washington objected to Cengic not just for his ties to Iran but his alleged obstruction of Croat-Moslem cooperation needed both to firm up the tenuous Federation and reunify Bosnia overall under terms of the 1995 Dayton peace treaty.
In Washington on Friday, U.S. sources said the dismissal of a second Federation defence official was also being sought.
U.S. sources did not identify that official, but Izetbegovic said it appeared to be Vladimir Soljic, a Croat who is Federation defence minister.
Izetbegovic said a U.S. State Department letter of September 19 cited "alleged non-cooperation of Cengic and Soljic". He did not say whether Soljic would also be removed.
Washington went public on Friday with its bid to have Cengic fired after discreet diplomatic efforts appeared to go nowhere.
